newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-DETROIT EXHULTS OVER STANLEY CUP, RED WINGS.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-DETROIT EXHULTS OVER STANLEY CUP, RED WINGS.

text.p: More than a million hockey fans gave their beloved Detroit Red Wings a thunderous welcome Tuesday in celebration of the team's first Stanley Cup victory in 42 years.

Throngs of red-and-white clad Detroiters filled downtown streets as Red Wings players, coaches and Lord Stanley's cup itself rolled past in red Ford Mustang convertibles accompanied by marching bands.

"This is great. We haven't had it for 42 years, and now the Cup is back in Detroit," said 10-year-old Matthew Porter, whose wait for the Cup was a lot shorter than many who came out to honour the NHL champions.
The Red Wings swept the Philadelphia Flyers in four games to win the Stanley Cup, capping a wild NHL playoff run with a 2-1 victory Saturday night.
Detroit was swept in the finals two years ago by the New Jersey Devils, one of many disappointments in the team's quest end the championship drought dating back to 1955.
"They had 42 years to plan it, I think they did a great job," legendary Detroit coach Scotty Bowman said of the celebration, attended by an estimated 1 million people.
"Boy, this beats playing in Philadelphia tonight for game five," he enthused.

Bowman, 63, who has won seven Stanley Cups with three different teams, said he will decide within two weeks whether he will retire on top or return as Wings' coach next season with an eye on an eighth Cup that would tie him with his idol, Toe Blake, for the NHL coaching record.

The silver cup -- hockey's Holy Grail and one of the oldest and most famous trophies in sports -- rode with team captain Steve Yzerman, who has spent his entire 14-season NHL career with the Red Wings.

New York City's Rockettes dance troupe adorned a float carrying a giant inflatable octopus, the Red Wings' unofficial mascot. Until the practice was outlawed this year, fans have traditionally tossed dead octopi onto the ice to celebrate Red Wings playoff goals, each leg representing how many wins it used to take to win the Stanley Cup. It now takes 16.

For Detroit, just as important as the winning the Stanley Cup was the city's ability to handle the victory celebration Saturday night without the violence that has marred past sports championships here.

Rioting and fires followed the Detroit Tigers' 1984 World Series victory and the NBA championship by the Detroit Pistons in 1990. But only about 20 people were arrested for disorderly conduct during the generally peaceful Red Wings celebration.
